contentHtml:
HAITI—The World Health Organization (WHO) has committed US$1 million to equip Hôpital Universitaire La Paix in Port-au-Prince, as it seeks to sustain healthcare delivery amid worsening insecurity and humanitarian pressures in the country.

WHO Director-General Dr Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus announced the funding during his visit to Haiti to reinforce the agency’s support for the country’s strained health system.

The investment will finance a computed tomography (CT) scanner and equipment for four operating rooms at the hospital.

The intervention targets one of the few major public referral hospitals still operating in Port-au-Prince, where healthcare facilities have been heavily affected by armed violence, displacement and supply disruptions.

Healthcare infrastructure under pressure

Nearly half of health facilities in Port-au-Prince are non-functional, with 49.5% closed and only 12% operating partially.

Across Haiti, which has a population of more than 11 million, 24.5% of health facilities are non-functional and 48.5% are operating partially.

Armed violence continues to disrupt healthcare access, forcing facilities to close, displacing communities and interrupting medical supply chains.

The displacement of approximately 1.5 million people has further strained services, while an estimated 4.9 million people require healthcare assistance in 2026.

“Haiti’s health system is under immense strain due to the overwhelming volume of patients and influx of trauma cases,” Dr Tedros said, following his visit to Hôpital Universitaire La Paix, where he observed the demands facing healthcare workers.

He reaffirmed WHO and the Pan American Health Organization (PAHO) support for the government and people of Haiti to maintain essential services, strengthen health infrastructure, improve disease surveillance and enhance outbreak response.

Hospital workload and WHO support

Since January 2026, Hôpital Universitaire La Paix has treated more than 19,575 emergency patients, including 291 people with gunshot wounds, performed 3,086 surgeries and managed 1,442 high-risk deliveries, with support from WHO and PAHO.

During the visit, Dr Tedros met Prime Minister Alix Didier Fils-Aimé, Minister of Public Health and Population Dr Bertrand Sinal, and United Nations partners to discuss priorities for strengthening the health system.

Over the past two years, WHO and PAHO have mobilised more than US$30 million to support Haiti’s health response.

The funding has helped sustain emergency care at key facilities, reduce cholera transmission and maintain essential services for vulnerable communities, while the agencies continue efforts to secure additional resources.

The latest funding comes days after WHO committed US$2 million to support Cuba’s national immunisation programme and healthcare delivery during Dr Tedros’ visit.

The investment in Haiti is expected to strengthen hospital capacity for emergency diagnostics, surgical procedures and critical care as healthcare providers contend with increasing patient needs and limited infrastructure.

Access to advanced diagnostic equipment and functioning operating rooms remains essential for maintaining referral services and managing trauma and other urgent conditions in crisis-affected settings.
